newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Waigel verbally defends mark amid EMU worry.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Waigel verbally defends mark amid EMU worry.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Tuesday abandoned all thoughts of the economic boost offered by a weak currency, acting instead to counter the view in currency markets that a strong mark is a thing of the past.

Waigel, speaking in Berlin, said Germany was interested in a strong mark, that markets had overreacted in pushing the dollar and sterling to multiple-year highs, and hinted that the Group of Seven could be prepared to take corrective action.

Analysts meanwhile blamed spats over European monetary union for the mark's weakness, claiming that the resultant verbal weakening of the entry criteria for monetary union had discredited both the planned euro and the mark itself.

In an indication of Germany's powerlessness to halt loose talk within Europe of the interpretational possibilities offered by the Maastricht Treaty, Waigel declined to comment on France's decreasing chances of matching the fiscal criteria.
Other major German politicians similarly avoided taking a hardline stance.

Waigel's support for the mark, which came hot on the heels of similar statements from Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer last week, barely braked the dollar as it soared to 71-month highs above 1.80 marks.

"We are interested in a strong deutschemark. I think what's happening at the moment is an overreaction of the markets," Waigel said in response to a question about the strength of the dollar and pound.
"We have, as in the past, agreed cooperation within the G7," he added, hinting the main industrial countries could take steps to boost the mark. "We are in contact with our partners."

The Group of Seven industrialised nations, which in 1995 called for an "orderly reversal" of the dollar from record lows near 1.3450 marks, signalled in February at a dollar rate of about 1.65 marks that the recovery had gone about far enough.
In April it repeated that message at a meeting in Washington, again seeking to stabilise the currency.

But analysts see current foreign exchange developments rooted less in dollar strength than in mark weakness linked to Europe's plans to launch a joint currency in 1999 under the terms laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.

"The statement from Waigel...shows the ignorance or perhaps helplessness of the administration of (Chancellor Helmut) Kohl with respect to the mark weakness, which has been triggered by the verbal loosening of the Maastricht criteria," analysts at ABN Amro said in a commentary.
"That means the mark weakness will continue," they added.
Thomas Mayer, chief economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt, agreed. "The exchange rate developments are disturbing. They demonstrate a certain mistrust in the government's EMU policy," he said.

Bonn has come under fire at home and abroad for pursuing a circular debate on the precise meaning of a Maastricht Treaty condition that countries entering monetary union should have a deficit of no more than three percent of total economic output.

German politicians as high up as Kohl himself have said on the record that this should be interpreted as 3.0 percent -- raising the further question of exactly how Germany's finances can be squeezed into the straitjacket of its own making.

But Bonn politicians showed a marked reluctance on Tuesday to comment on France's battle to qualify for the euro despite continued uncertainty over whether Paris can make the grade or is willing even to make the efforts necessary to do so.

For the second time in the past few days, Waigel sidestepped a question on whether Paris could meet the criteria, saying all countries, including France, had agreed everyone must do their own homework.

Even Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, a fierce advocate of strictly interpreting the criteria, appeared to hold his fire while Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel hinted strongly he favoured exploiting room for manoeuvre in the Maastricht Treaty.
President Jacques Chirac said on Monday France was now running a budget deficit of around 3.5 percent of GDP.
